section.title: Comfort for the Contrite
section.sectionRationale: Right after promising a house of prayer for all nations, Isaiah turns to indict Israel's own failed shepherds and idolatrous people, blind watchmen, greedy dogs, child sacrifice in the valleys, before landing on one of the most tender verses in the whole book, the High and Lofty One who dwells with the contrite and lowly in spirit. It is judgment and comfort in the same breath.
section.thesis: God exposes Israel's failed shepherds and shameless idolatry without flinching, yet the same high and holy God who inhabits eternity chooses to dwell with the crushed and lowly in spirit, promising peace to those far and near while insisting there is no peace for the wicked.
section.frameNote: Four movements: blind watchmen and greedy shepherds; the righteous perishing unnoticed; Israel's shameless idolatry exposed; and the High and Lofty One who dwells with the contrite, offering peace, peace to those far and near.

verses.text: Come, all you beasts of the field; eat greedily, all you beasts of the forest.
Israel’s watchmen are blind, they are all oblivious; they are all mute dogs, they cannot bark; they are dreamers lying around, loving to slumber.
Like ravenous dogs, they are never satisfied. They are shepherds with no discernment; they all turn to their own way, each one seeking his own gain:
“Come, let me get the wine, let us imbibe the strong drink, and tomorrow will be like today, only far better!”

units.label: The righteous perish, no one takes it to heart
units.note: guided from the presence of evil

verses.text: The righteous perish, and no one takes it to heart; devout men are swept away, while no one considers that the righteous are guided from the presence of evil.
Those who walk uprightly enter into peace; they find rest, lying down in death.

units.label: Sons of a sorceress
units.note: idolatry, child sacrifice, exhausting pursuit of false gods

verses.text: “But come here, you sons of a sorceress, you offspring of adulterers and prostitutes!
Whom are you mocking? At whom do you snarl and stick out your tongue? Are you not children of transgression, offspring of deceit,
who burn with lust among the oaks, under every luxuriant tree, who slaughter your children in the valleys, under the clefts of the rocks?
Your portion is among the smooth stones of the valley; indeed, they are your lot. Even to them you have poured out a drink offering and offered a grain offering. Should I relent because of these?
On a high and lofty hill you have made your bed, and there you went up to offer sacrifices.

Behind the door and doorpost you have set up your memorial. Forsaking Me, you uncovered your bed; you climbed up and opened it wide. And you have made a pact with those whose bed you have loved; you have gazed upon their nakedness.
You went to Molech with oil and multiplied your perfumes. You have sent your envoys a great distance; you have descended even to Sheol itself.
You are wearied by your many journeys, but you did not say, “There is no hope!” You found renewal of your strength; therefore you did not grow weak.
Whom have you dreaded and feared, so that you lied and failed to remember Me or take this to heart? Is it not because I have long been silent that you do not fear Me?
I will expose your righteousness and your works, and they will not profit you.

When you cry out, let your companies of idols deliver you! Yet the wind will carry off all of them, a breath will take them away. But he who seeks refuge in Me will inherit the land and possess My holy mountain.”

units.label: I dwell with the contrite in spirit
units.note: peace, peace to those far and near

verses.text: And it will be said, “Build it up, build it up, prepare the way, take every obstacle out of the way of My people.”

For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: “I dwell in a high and holy place, and with the oppressed and {{shafal|humble}} in spirit, to restore the spirit of the lowly and revive the heart of the {{nidkeh|contrite}}.
For I will not accuse you forever, nor will I always be angry; for then the spirit of man would grow weak before Me, with the breath of those I have made.
I was enraged by his sinful greed, so I struck him and hid My face in anger; yet he kept turning back to the desires of his heart.
I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will guide him and restore comfort to him and his mourners,
bringing praise to their lips. Peace, peace to those far and near,” says the LORD, “and I will heal them.”
But the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea, for it cannot be still, and its waves churn up mire and muck.
“There is no peace,” says my God, “for the wicked.”

shafal.gloss: Humble, low, brought down. God, who is Himself high and lifted up, chooses deliberately to dwell with the one who is shaphal, low in spirit, an intentional condescension of the exalted God toward the humbled soul, the same movement Paul later describes of Christ, Philippians 2:8.

nidkeh.gloss: Crushed, contrite, struck down in spirit. God revives the heart of the nakeh, the one crushed by grief or guilt; the same root and idea appears in Psalm 34:18, the LORD is near to the brokenhearted, and shapes Jesus' own beatitude, blessed are the poor in spirit, Matthew 5:3.

basic.context: Isaiah moves from Israel's failed leaders, watchmen too blind to warn and shepherds too greedy to care, to shocking idolatry, child sacrifice and shrine prostitution among the very people who claimed God's name. Yet the chapter turns, without losing its honesty about sin, to one of the tenderest promises in the book: the high and holy God dwells with the crushed and lowly.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage refuses to soften either truth: sin is named plainly and without excuse, watchmen who cannot bark, sacrifice to Molech, yet God's nearness to the humble is offered just as plainly, without conditions of achievement, only brokenness and turning to Him. It closes with a stark, unremovable line, there is no peace for the wicked, that must be held alongside the comfort.
basic.originalLanguages: God is described dwelling with the shafal, the humble and brought-low, and reviving the heart of the nidkeh, the crushed or contrite. These are not abstractions; they describe real people, brought low by real guilt or grief, whom the eternal God stoops to meet.
basic.typology: The high and lofty One who dwells with the lowly anticipates the incarnation itself, God taking on lowliness to dwell among the humble, and the peace, peace to those far and near anticipates the peace Christ makes between Jew and Gentile at the cross.
basic.christ: Paul quotes this exact phrase, peace to those who were far and peace to those who were near, in Ephesians 2:17, applying it directly to the peace Christ achieves between Jew and Gentile through His blood. Jesus' own beatitude, blessed are the poor in spirit, and blessed are those who mourn, Matthew 5:3-4, echoes the promise that God restores the lowly and comforts mourners.
basic.god: God does not deny His own anger at persistent, self-destructive sin, I was enraged, I struck him, yet He insists He will not accuse forever, choosing instead to heal, guide, and comfort those who turn back to Him, a holiness that judges and a nearness that restores held together without contradiction.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 2:17 quotes this passage of the peace Christ brings to those far and near. Psalm 34:18 echoes God's nearness to the brokenhearted and crushed in spirit. Matthew 5:3-4 pictures the same comfort for the poor in spirit and those who mourn.
basic.oneStory: God exposes His people's worst failures without flinching, then still stoops from His high and holy dwelling to revive the crushed and comfort the mourner. That same movement, holiness descending to dwell with the humble, reaches its fullness when God becomes flesh in Christ and makes peace for those far and near at the cross.

context.literary:
The passage is a sequence of four sharp turns, and each is cued by a word. It opens with a call, 'Come, all you beasts of the field,' Isaiah 56:9, and the same word 'come' returns twice more, in the drinkers' invitation of verse 12, 'Come, let me get the wine,' and in God's summons to the idolaters, 'But come here, you sons of a sorceress,' Isaiah 57:3. These calls turn a deliberate echo against Isaiah 55:1, where God had said 'Come, buy wine and milk without money.' The leaders offer a counter-invitation to a drinking party, and the God of Isaiah 55 invites the accused to court.

The first block, 56:9-12, is a satire on leaders: watchmen who cannot bark, shepherds who cannot see. The second, 57:1-2, is a brief sad reflection on the righteous who die unnoticed. The third, 57:3-13, is a prosecution speech with a run of 'you' verbs, a cultic catalogue of lust, child sacrifice, pilgrimage and diplomacy, ending in the verdict that the idols will be carried off by the wind. The fourth, 57:14-21, turns on a call to build a road, as in Isaiah 40:3, and then on the speech of the One who inhabits eternity.

Two word-pairs organize the turn. The hill the idolaters climb is 'high and lofty,' verse 7, and the One they ignore is 'high and lifted up,' verse 15, with the same two Hebrew terms behind both. The peace theme brackets the chapter: the upright 'enter into peace,' 57:2, God offers 'Peace, peace' in 57:19, and the section closes with the refrain that there is no peace for the wicked, verse 21, the same line that ended an earlier section in Isaiah 48:22.
context.historical:
The abuses described belong to a period when Judah's leaders and worship were thoroughly compromised. The watchmen are the prophets and teachers who were supposed to sound the alarm, as Ezekiel was commissioned to do, Ezekiel 3:17-18, and the shepherds are the rulers and priests whom Ezekiel 34 and Jeremiah 23:1-2 condemn for feeding themselves. The line that tomorrow will be 'like today, only far better,' verse 12, is the voice of a ruling class that was unconcerned about judgment, much like those who say in Micah 3:11, 'No disaster can come upon us.'

The worship in verses 3 to 13 matches what the histories and prophets describe in the worst eras. Under King Manasseh, who reigned for fifty-five years, there were altars to Baal and the host of heaven, sorcery and divination, and the king 'sacrificed his own son in the fire,' 2 Kings 21:1-6. Child sacrifice was practiced at Topheth in the valley of Hinnom, Jeremiah 7:30-31, and the law had forbidden giving children to Molech, Leviticus 18:21. Hosea describes worship under oaks and terebinths because the shade is pleasant, Hosea 4:13. The mention of Sheol and the envoys sent a great distance, verse 9, may refer to diplomacy with foreign powers, a habit the prophet rebukes elsewhere, Isaiah 30:1-2 and 31:1, or to consulting the dead, Isaiah 8:19, or to both.

Scholars differ on when this was spoken. Some place it in the monarchy, near Manasseh's time, and others in the years after the return from exile. The text does not give a date, and the message holds either way. The BSB notes that the word translated 'Molech' in verse 9 can also be read 'the king,' a reminder that even the translation is not settled.
context.canonical:
Verses 9 to 12 gather up a long line of prophetic complaint about unfaithful leaders: shepherds who feed themselves, Ezekiel 34:1-10, and who dress the wound of the people lightly, Jeremiah 6:13-14, and the worthless shepherd who deserts the flock, Zechariah 11:17. The answer in each case is that God Himself will shepherd, and that He will raise up one shepherd, Ezekiel 34:23. Jesus takes that role when He calls Himself the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11.

The portrait of God in verse 15 recalls Isaiah's own vision, 'the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted,' Isaiah 6:1. The surprise is that He also dwells with the humble, which the book repeats in its closing chapter: 'This is the one I will esteem: he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word,' Isaiah 66:2. The psalms say the same, 'The LORD is near to the brokenhearted,' Psalm 34:18, and 'a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise,' Psalm 51:17.

The word of peace in verse 19 is taken up by Paul, who says Christ 'came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near,' Ephesians 2:17. The picture of God dwelling with the lowly leads to Revelation's promise that 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3. Jesus' own blessings on the poor in spirit and those who mourn, Matthew 5:3-4, and the tax collector who goes home justified, Luke 18:13-14, belong to the same line.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet wants his hearers to see that there are two kinds of people before God and to know which they are. For the leaders and the idolaters he writes with open contempt, using the terms of the courtroom and the street, because euphemism would have let them continue. The accusation that the leaders are blind and drunk and that the people are making private shrines is meant to break the illusion that tomorrow will be like today, verse 12.

He also wants the contrite to be able to hear. The abrupt turn in verse 14 and the speech of the Holy One in verse 15 are for those who were crushed by the very failures just described, who had suffered under bad leaders, and who were worried that God's anger was permanent. They are told it is not. The explanation in verse 16 gives God's own reason for limiting His wrath, that He remembers the frailty of what He made.

The effect is intentionally two-edged. Those who read verses 3 to 13 and recognize themselves are urged to take refuge in God, who promises that 'he who seeks refuge in Me will inherit the land,' verse 13. Those who recognize themselves in verses 15 to 19 are told they are wanted. The chapter allows no one to hear comfort without also hearing truth, and no one to hear judgment without also hearing the open door.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The graphic scenes of verses 3 to 9 are description. They record what Judah did, and they are not a template or an endorsement. The sins of verse 5, burning with lust among the oaks and slaughtering children, are named so that readers will recoil, and the application is not to find parallel practices to condemn in others but to ask which gods we serve and which refuges we run to.

Verse 15 is a promise and not a technique. It does not say that if a person manufactures humility God will visit. It says that this is where God already lives, among the oppressed and the crushed, and that He revives them. Humility is not a payment for His company but the condition of those who know they need it. Neither does it mean the proud are beyond reach. The call in verse 13 to take refuge in God is open to everyone.

Verses 1 and 2 describe an observation and should be handled gently. They speak of the righteous who die and are not noticed, and say that they are 'guided from the presence of evil' and 'find rest.' That is a comfort for a particular situation, in which a righteous person is taken before disaster, as King Josiah was told he would be, 2 Kings 22:20. It is not a rule that every early death is a mercy, and it should not be used to answer every grief.

debates.question: What does it mean that 'the righteous perish' in verses 1 and 2?

views.label: Death as a merciful removal from coming disaster
views.case: The righteous are 'guided from the presence of evil' and 'enter into peace,' as if God takes them before the calamity falls. This is the pattern in 2 Kings 22:20, where Josiah is told he will be gathered to his grave in peace so that his eyes will not see the coming disaster. On this reading the verse is a comfort.

views.label: A complaint about the death of the faithful through persecution
views.case: Manasseh 'shed so much innocent blood that he filled Jerusalem from end to end,' 2 Kings 21:16, and the prophet may have in view righteous people killed by an unjust regime while no one took it to heart. The verse then describes a scandal, with the rest as the answer of God that these deaths are not final.

views.label: Both a scandal and a comfort
views.case: The two lines of the verse hold both. People overlook the righteous as they die, which is the scandal. God knows their end and brings them to rest, which is the comfort.

debates.bearing: All three agree that God is not blind to the death of the righteous, even if no one else notices, and that death for them leads to peace, which sets up the whole contrast with the wicked at the end of the chapter.

debates.question: Who are those 'far and near' who receive peace in verse 19?

views.label: Jews at home and Jews in exile
views.case: Daniel speaks of 'all Israel near and far, in all the countries to which You have driven us,' Daniel 9:7. On this reading, those near are the people in the land and those far are the scattered exiles, all brought into peace.

views.label: Jews and Gentiles
views.case: The previous chapters of Isaiah have welcomed the foreigner who joins himself to the LORD, Isaiah 56:3-8, and promised nations will run to Israel, Isaiah 55:5. Paul reads the verse this way, applying it to Gentiles who were far away and Jews who were near, Ephesians 2:17.

views.label: Both, in a widening circle
views.case: The phrase may describe all of God's people wherever they are, with the New Testament showing that this includes the nations. The Hebrew puts 'far' first, which has been noticed by many readers.

debates.bearing: Paul's use is an authorized extension of Isaiah's wording, not a contradiction of it. The peace that is offered to the scattered of Israel is offered through the same work to the Gentiles as well.

study.originalLanguages:
The leaders of verses 10 and 11 are called 'ravenous dogs,' and the Hebrew is 'dogs strong of appetite.' The word for appetite is nefesh, the usual word for the self or soul, here in its older sense of throat and craving. These men are described as all appetite. Of the shepherds the verse says they have 'no discernment,' lo yade'u havin, using the root bin, to understand or discriminate. They lack the very faculty that shepherds are supposed to exercise. The same self-seeking is summed up in 'each one seeking his own gain,' and the toast of verse 12, 'tomorrow will be like today,' is the voice of such people.

In verse 8 the accusation gets domestic. 'Behind the door and doorpost you have set up your memorial.' The word for doorpost is mezuzah, the same word used in Deuteronomy 6:9, where God's people are to write His words on the doorposts of their houses. The word for memorial, zikkaron, belongs to the language of remembrance. The idolaters have taken the place where God's word was to be written and put their own emblem there. Verse 6 adds a wordplay that does not survive English. The 'smooth stones of the valley' use the Hebrew chalaq, and the 'portion' that the stones have is cheleq, words that sound nearly alike. The wording suggests that the people have taken the stones as their allotted share, where they should have taken the LORD.

The central verse, 15, sets two phrases against the preceding verses. The LORD is 'high and lifted up,' ram venissa, the exact phrase used of the Lord on His throne in Isaiah 6:1, and the idolaters had climbed a mountain 'high and lofty,' gavoah venissa, in verse 7, with the same second word. They go up to find a god, and the God they bypassed lives above them yet comes down. He 'inhabits eternity,' shoken ad, from shakan, the root of mishkan, the tabernacle and of His promise 'that I may dwell among them,' Exodus 25:8. He lives in a high and holy place and also with the lowly, 'the oppressed and humble in spirit.'

Verses 18 and 19 gather a cluster of words for healing and comfort. The verb rapha, to heal, is used in 'I will heal him' and again in 'I will heal them,' framing the promise. The word for comfort, nichumim, is from the root that gave the opening of the book's second half, 'Comfort, comfort My people,' Isaiah 40:1. The long section that began with that promise reaches it again here at its darkest point. And 'Peace, peace,' shalom shalom, uses the doubled form that also lies behind 'perfect peace' in Isaiah 26:3, as if peace is spoken twice for completeness.

typology.type: The High and Lofty One who dwells with the lowly, verse 15
typology.fulfillment: The God who inhabits eternity and lives with the crushed is seen in the Son who 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, whose name Immanuel means 'God with us,' Matthew 1:23. Paul describes how He, existing in the form of God, emptied Himself and humbled Himself to death on a cross, Philippians 2:6-8. The correspondence is exact in direction: the One who is high comes down. The escalation is that Isaiah promised a nearness of presence, while the Gospel records a nearness of flesh. The type falls short because it describes where God lives and not yet who He became.

typology.type: Peace, peace to those far and near, verse 19
typology.fulfillment: Paul reads the promise as fulfilled in Christ, who 'is our peace,' and who 'came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near,' Ephesians 2:14-17. Isaiah's earlier word on the Servant said the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, Isaiah 53:5, and Paul says we 'have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,' Romans 5:1. Jesus gives a peace that the world cannot, John 14:27. The type falls short because Isaiah's peace is promised and Paul's is already given, with the final peace still to come.

typology.type: The blind watchmen and greedy shepherds, 56:10-11
typology.fulfillment: This is a contrast and not a prefiguring. The hired hand who runs away when the wolf comes, John 10:12, resembles the faithless leaders, and the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, is their opposite. Ezekiel 34:23 had promised that God would appoint one shepherd, a servant like David, and Jesus takes that role. The pattern falls short in that leaders can still fail, and the church is told to watch and guard, which makes the final vindication of the true Shepherd the real hope.

typology.type: God's anger and the healing that follows, verses 17 and 18
typology.fulfillment: God says He struck His people and hid His face, and then that He will heal them. At the cross Jesus cried, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46, and Peter says that He bore our sins in His body on the tree and that 'By His stripes you are healed,' 1 Peter 2:24, quoting Isaiah 53:5. The hiding of the face and the wound are not abolished but borne. This is an echo and a development and not an exact parallel. The type falls short because Isaiah promises healing, and the cross shows the price at which it comes.

typology.type: The contrite one who is received, verse 15
typology.fulfillment: The one God revives is the crushed and humble in spirit. Jesus gives this a face in a parable of two men in the temple. The tax collector who beats his breast and says, 'God, have mercy on me, a sinner!' goes home justified, Luke 18:13-14. This is a pattern, not a prediction, and it holds that the humble are the ones God receives. Hebrews adds the grounds: we have a high priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses, so we can approach the throne of grace with confidence, Hebrews 4:15-16. The pattern falls short on its own, since it is the High Priest who makes approach possible.

study.christ:
The most direct line is Paul's. In Ephesians 2:17 he writes that Christ 'came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near,' and the wording is the wording of Isaiah 57:19. For Paul the promise of peace to the far and near is not simply an echo but a prophecy that has been kept. The cross is how, as he says, Christ has 'made the two one' and 'reconciled both of them to God in one body,' Ephesians 2:14-16. Isaiah has just welcomed the foreigner, and here the God who gathers the outcasts promises peace to those who are far. Colossians says the same, that He made peace 'through the blood of His cross,' Colossians 1:20.

The chapter also leads to Christ in the direction of the descent. The prophet describes a God who is not content to stay in His high and holy place but who also dwells with the contrite. John says the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and Philippians traces the way down: He did not cling to equality with God but emptied Himself and took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-7. Jesus also says of Himself, 'I am gentle and humble in heart,' and invites the weary and burdened to come to Him for rest, Matthew 11:28-29. The Holy One who lives with the lowly comes to be among them.

It leads to Christ in His treatment of the failed leaders. The chapter's picture of shepherds who feed themselves is answered when Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd who lays down His life, John 10:11, in contrast with the one who 'runs away because he is a hired servant,' John 10:13. Ezekiel had said God would appoint one shepherd over His flock, Ezekiel 34:23, and Jesus gathers that promise to Himself.

It leads to Christ in what He does with the anger and the face that is hidden. In verse 17 God says He struck His people and hid His face, and in verse 18 that He will heal. The healing does not come by pretending the anger was not real. The Servant of the previous chapters was 'crushed for our iniquities,' and 'by His stripes we are healed,' Isaiah 53:5, and Peter reads that of Christ, 1 Peter 2:24. On the cross He cries out the language of the hidden face, Matthew 27:46. The mercy of verse 16, that God will not accuse forever, rests on the fact that someone bore the accusation.

A caution keeps this honest. The sorceress and the oaks and the smooth stones are not riddles about Jesus, and the passage should not be forced to speak of Him in every phrase. Its witness is strongest where the New Testament itself picks it up, in the peace to the far and near and in the pattern of God coming down. It also tells us what kind of person He receives. Jesus blesses the poor in spirit and those who mourn, Matthew 5:3-4, and the Christ who invites them is the One who does the reviving of verse 15.
study.god:
The God of this passage is introduced by His address, and the address is paradoxical. He is 'high and lifted up,' the One 'who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy,' and He lives 'in a high and holy place' and also with the crushed. These are not two different gods or two moods. The same loftiness is the reason He can stoop without loss. The prophet's vision in Isaiah 6:1 and the promise here describe one throne. Hebrews speaks of the same union when it says we have a high priest who is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, Hebrews 4:15.

He is a God of real anger. Verse 17 does not soften it: 'I was enraged by his sinful greed, so I struck him and hid My face in anger.' The sin is named plainly, and the discipline is real. The silence of God in verse 11 is also described. The idolaters have misread His long silence as indifference, and they no longer fear Him. Paul speaks of this when he asks whether people disregard 'the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God's kindness leads you to repentance,' Romans 2:4. God's patience is not the same as approval.

He is also a God who limits His own anger for the sake of the creature. Verse 16 says, 'I will not accuse you forever, nor will I always be angry; for then the spirit of man would grow weak before Me.' God is not ruled by His wrath. He is mindful of the frailty of what He has made, as Psalm 103:14 says, 'He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust.' Anger has its place, but it does not have the last word.

He is a God who initiates mercy in the face of persistent failure. The man in verse 17 'kept turning back to the desires of his heart,' and yet God says, 'I have seen his ways, but I will heal him.' It is not that the man earned it. The 'but' is God's, and each verb that follows, heal, guide, restore, bring, is a promise God makes without being asked.

He is also the only refuge. The idols are carried off by the wind, and the one who takes refuge in God inherits the land and the holy mountain, verse 13. The moral order He keeps is stable, and the wicked who refuse Him are like a sea that cannot be still, with nothing at rest.

For worship, the chapter says that approach to this God is not by climbing. The idolaters went up a high hill to find a god. The true God is higher than any hill, and He comes down. The right response is to bring nothing but the need, as the contrite do, and to trust the One who restores the spirit of the lowly.

crossReferences.note: Ezekiel's charge against the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves, fail to strengthen the weak and let the flock scatter is the fuller form of Isaiah 56:10-11. Both prophets end with God Himself taking the flock from their hands, which is the background for Jesus as the good shepherd.

The prophets and priests dress the wound of the people lightly, saying 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace. It exposes the false word of peace that Isaiah's watchmen offer. The peace of Isaiah 57:19 is a different kind, spoken by the God who heals the wound.

Isaiah sees the Lord on a throne, high and exalted. The phrase is the same as 'high and lifted up' in Isaiah 57:15, which is deliberate. The One the prophet saw in the temple is the One who stoops to the contrite, and the vision of holiness and the promise of nearness belong together.

The book's last chapter puts the same truth another way. Heaven is God's throne and earth His footstool, so no house can contain Him, and the one He esteems is 'he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word.' It confirms that Isaiah 57:15 is not an aside but a theme.

The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the contrite in spirit. The psalm puts in a line what Isaiah 57:15 says in a full speech, and it shows that this was a settled part of Israel's worship, sung by those who had learned to expect God in their lowest moments.

David, after his sin, says God does not want sacrifice for its own sake but 'a broken and a contrite heart.' Isaiah 57:15 draws on the same family of words for the crushed and contrite. The man who has sinned most openly is told that this is the offering God will not despise.

The refrain 'There is no peace for the wicked' appears here at the close of an earlier section, and again in 57:21. It marks a repeated boundary in the book, so that every large movement of comfort is accompanied by a reminder of what remains outside it.

The account of Manasseh, who rebuilt the high places, set up altars to the host of heaven, practiced sorcery and sacrificed his son in the fire. It supplies the kind of background that explains the accusations of verses 3 to 9, and shows they are not poetic exaggeration.

Paul says those 'far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ,' and that Christ 'preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near.' He reads Isaiah 57:19 as a promise kept at the cross, with Jew and Gentile reconciled to God in one body.

As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him, for He knows our frame and is mindful that we are dust. It is the same reasoning as Isaiah 57:16, that God limits His anger because He remembers what He made.

We have a high priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses, and so may approach the throne of grace with confidence. It gives the ground for the promise of Isaiah 57:15, since the High and Lofty One is also the one who has shared our weakness, and the contrite may come to Him.

The dwelling place of God is with man, and He will wipe away every tear, with no more death, mourning, crying or pain. It is the full form of Isaiah 57:15, in which the high God dwells with His people, and it answers the mourners of 57:18 who are comforted at last.

study.oneStory:
The story begins with a God who walks in a garden and a man who hides, and God's first words to him are a question, 'Where are you?' Genesis 3:8-9. The movement of the whole Bible is the gap between the heights and the hiding, between a God who comes looking and people who climb, run or conceal. Isaiah 57 shows both movements in one chapter. The people go up a high and lofty hill and sink to Sheol itself, in search of something that will save them, and meanwhile the One who is high and lifted up gives a different address.

The pattern of human ascent first shows in Babel, where people said, 'let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens,' and the LORD 'came down to see,' Genesis 11:4-5. The prophets then show the same pattern in Israel's alliances and idols. Every attempt to build a ladder ends with God descending. Isaiah 57:15 gives that descent a character. The God who comes down does so not just to inspect but to dwell, and the one He dwells with is the one who knows he cannot climb.

This chapter also takes the book of Isaiah to a turning point. The long promise of comfort that began in Isaiah 40 had to deal with a people who still preferred their idols and their leaders their own gain. The answer is not that the promise is withdrawn but that it is offered to a particular kind of person, the contrite, and that the Servant's work in Isaiah 53 will be the means. The leaders who fail are answered in Jesus, who lays down His life for the sheep.

The New Testament shows the descent in the incarnation, in Christ coming to the far and the near and making peace by His blood, and in the church, which is the place where God now dwells among the humble by His Spirit. The chapter's last line, that there is no peace for the wicked, remains true, and the story does not hide it. The book of Revelation also keeps the boundary, that those who refuse remain outside.

The end of the story is the fulfillment of verse 15 in full. The One who is high and holy lives with His people, 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3, and He wipes every tear from their eyes, Revelation 21:4. The same chapter says 'the sea was no more,' Revelation 21:1. That image of a restless sea does not belong to the new creation, which fits well with the picture in verse 20 of the wicked as a sea that cannot be still. In that world the restless find rest and the mourners are comforted, and the holy God no longer needs to descend because He is already at home with them.

sermon.title: Grace Amid Frailty: God's Presence with the Broken
sermon.why: Carson works through Isaiah 56-57 in three portraits, a righteous God who welcomes contrite sinners, an idolatrous people, and the promise of God's presence with the broken, centering on 57:15's picture of the transcendent God who dwells with the contrite and lowly in spirit, the heart of this passage.

quiz.q: What failure does Isaiah name in Israel's watchmen and shepherds, 56:9-12?

options.text: They are blind, silent, self-seeking, and given to drunken pleasure instead of warning and guarding the people.
options.note: Verses 10-12 describe watchmen who cannot bark and shepherds seeking only their own gain.

options.text: They are too strict in enforcing God's law.
options.note: The failure is neglect and self-indulgence, not excessive strictness.

options.text: They are too young and inexperienced to lead.
options.note: The text describes moral failure, not inexperience.

options.text: They are persecuted for warning the people too much.
options.note: This is the opposite of what the text says; they fail to warn at all, described as mute dogs who cannot bark.

quiz.q: What does God mean by saying He dwells 'with the oppressed and humble in spirit,' 57:15?

options.text: The high and holy God chooses to draw near and revive those who are crushed and lowly in spirit.
options.note: The verse pairs God's transcendence with His deliberate nearness to the humble.

options.text: God only associates with the powerful and self-sufficient.
options.note: The verse says the opposite; He dwells with the lowly and contrite.

options.text: God is physically confined to a single earthly location.
options.note: The verse emphasizes His transcendence, inhabiting eternity, alongside His chosen nearness.

options.text: It refers only to God's presence in the Jerusalem temple.
options.note: The temple is one place God's presence dwelt, but this verse speaks of God's posture toward the humble in spirit generally, not one building.

quiz.q: How does Paul use Isaiah 57:19, 'peace, peace to those far and near,' in Ephesians 2?

options.text: He applies it to Christ's work of reconciling Jew and Gentile into one people through His blood.
options.note: Ephesians 2:14-17 quotes this phrase directly of Christ's peace-making work.

options.text: He applies it only to physical distance between cities.
options.note: Paul applies it to spiritual reconciliation, not literal geography.

options.text: He uses it to argue that Gentiles remain permanently excluded from God's people.
options.note: This is the opposite of Paul's whole argument, which is full inclusion of Gentiles through Christ's peace.

quiz.q: How does the passage close in 57:20-21, and why does it matter?

options.text: It insists there is no peace for the wicked, holding judgment and comfort together without contradiction.
options.note: The promise of comfort to the contrite does not erase the reality of judgment for the unrepentant.

options.text: It promises peace to everyone regardless of repentance.
options.note: The text explicitly denies peace to the wicked who do not turn.

options.text: It contradicts the earlier promise of healing in verse 18-19.
options.note: It can read as tension, but the two truths sit together consistently: healing for those who turn, no peace for those who refuse.

options.text: It refers only to a temporary lack of political peace, not spiritual standing.
options.note: The context is about spiritual restoration and refusal, not merely politics.

questions: Israel's watchmen were blind and silent when they should have warned. Where might you be staying silent when you should be speaking up in love?

The chapter names Israel's idolatry in raw, uncomfortable detail. What is the modern equivalent chase, the exhausting pursuit of something that leaves you wearied but unwilling to admit there is no hope in it?
God says He dwells with the contrite and lowly in spirit. Are you trying to appear strong before God rather than coming to Him crushed and honest?
Peace, peace to those far and near is fulfilled in Christ reconciling Jew and Gentile. Who feels far from you, or far from God, that you could help draw near through the peace of Christ?
The chapter ends starkly, there is no peace for the wicked. Is there an area of ongoing, unrepented sin in your life quietly robbing you of the peace God offers to the contrite?

translationNotes.note: Molech was the Ammonite deity associated with child sacrifice, condemned repeatedly in the Torah, Leviticus 18:21, 20:2-5; the reference here confirms Israel's absorption of this practice despite the law's clear prohibition.
High and lofty renders the same Hebrew phrase used of the LORD Himself in 6:1, deliberately echoing Isaiah's own inaugural vision of God's transcendence, now paired with His nearness to the lowly.
